assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theory predicted flat bands at a magic twist angle and experiments then found correlated insulators and superconductivity in a tunable, clean platform. It opened moire quantum materials as a whole field and gives a transparent, controllable setting for strongly correlated many-body physics, which I find compelling as a statistical physicist.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model is the decisive theory; the 2018 Jarillo-Herrero group experiments are the decisive discovery of the correlated phases. Eva Andrei's early STM and transport work on twisted layers is also important, so a three-person split leaves someone out.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups and extended to other moire systems; the superconducting pairing mechanism is still debated, but the core phenomena are firmly established. Recognition is timely, with the risk that the field is still moving quickly.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved.
Fair credit to Andrei and other early experimentalists is debatable.
Whether the prize should wait for more settled consequences of the field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock with magic-wavelength trapping combines many atoms with extreme coherence and reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. It is a clear invention with lasting impact on metrology, tests of fundamental physics and a possible redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first realizations; Ye's group pushed accuracy and stability to record levels. Two laureates fit well, though the 2005 and 2012 prizes already touched on frequency combs and trapped-ion clocks, and others in the clock community made major contributions.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by multiple independent laboratories worldwide and used in international comparisons. Timing is very good and mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier prizes on optical frequency metrology.
Contributions of other clock groups, for example in Sr and Yb systems, could be debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory gives a controlled, nonperturbative treatment of strong local correlations in the infinite-dimension limit and underlies the modern theory of Mott transitions and correlated materials. It is conceptually original and widely used, in the spirit of statistical mean-field methods.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt's infinite-dimension limit and Georges and Kotliar's mapping to an impurity problem are decisive; Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt cover the main conceptual line. Contributions by Muller-Hartmann and Jarrell, and by Kuramoto and others, complicate a clean allocation, and the proposed list leaves out Metzner.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed over three decades by comparison with experiment and numerics in cuprates, vanadates and heavy-fermion materials, although quantitative predictive power for real materials is mixed. Mature and arguably overdue for recognition.
uncertainties: Credit allocation involving Metzner and Muller-Hartmann.
Predictive success for real materials is uneven and not independent of the DFT+DMFT extensions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators established a new classification of band insulators, with robust edge or surface conduction, and the quantum spin Hall and quantum anomalous Hall effects were realized experimentally. The conceptual breakthrough and the experimental demonstration are both important and lastingly influential.
assessment.attribution: Kane (with Mele) supplied the Z2 theory, Molenkamp's group realized the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and Xue's group observed the quantum anomalous Hall effect. The theory credit is split among Kane, Mele, Bernevig, Zhang, Fu and Moore, and not all are available in this entry, so the fit is imperfect.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed across materials and by ARPES and transport; the field is mature. Applications remain limited but the conceptual impact is clear.
uncertainties: Compound discovery whose theory and experiment parts may need different recognition.
Mele and Hasan are credited in a competing entry, which makes this configuration contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fluctuation theorems and the Jarzynski equality give exact relations for work and entropy production far from equilibrium, extending thermodynamics to small, fluctuating systems. As someone working with stochastic processes I regard this as a significant, clear and widely applicable result, tested in single-molecule experiments.
assessment.attribution: Jarzynski's work equality and the Evans-Searles and Gallavotti-Cohen theorems are central, and Crooks contributed the detailed fluctuation theorem. Bochkov and Kuzovlev, Gallavotti, Cohen, Searles and others have claims not represented here, so allocation is unsettled; I propose Jarzynski and Evans only.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in optical-tweezer and RNA-pulling experiments by Bustamante and others, and used in free-energy estimation. Mature, though the impact is more on theory and methodology than on a discovery of new phenomena.
uncertainties: Experimental confirmers are not in the credited names.
Importance outside nonequilibrium theory is less certain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED provides strong light-matter coupling with superconducting artificial atoms and is the architecture behind much superconducting quantum computing. It is a clear and highly influential invention.
assessment.attribution: Blais and colleagues proposed it, Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling in 2004. This is a clean three-person structure, though the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits overlaps in domain and may reduce near-term appetite.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in many laboratories and widely used; the technology is still evolving, so some of its eventual impact is not yet settled.
uncertainties: Proximity to the recent prize for superconducting-circuit quantum effects.
Role of other circuit pioneers such as Nakamura or Devoret in credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Energy-landscape and funnel ideas, rooted in spin-glass physics, explain how proteins fold quickly despite a huge conformational space. This is an elegant application of statistical physics to biological matter and has shaped how the problem is understood.
assessment.attribution: Wolynes and Onuchic developed the funnel and minimal-frustration picture, and Dill contributed the hydrophobic-collapse and lattice-model line. Bryngelson, Wolynes and others were also decisive, so credit is somewhat diffuse.
assessment.maturity: Broadly accepted as a conceptual framework, though predictive tests are indirect and the field has been shaped by computation and machine learning. Whether it is physics as opposed to chemistry or biology is a legitimate concern.
uncertainties: Disciplinary fit for the physics prize.
Credit also belongs to Bryngelson and others outside the list.
Recent machine-learning advances in protein structure may overshadow it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realize Hubbard-type models and enable controlled many-body quantum simulation, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition. They bridge statistical and condensed-matter physics with atomic physics, with lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and colleagues proposed the Hubbard realization, Greiner, Bloch and Hansch observed the Mott transition, and Esslinger and Bloch developed fermionic and other extensions. Five credited names exceed a three-person limit, so selection necessarily excludes major contributors.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed and mature, with a growing set of analog quantum simulators. Some of the field has been recognized through earlier ultracold-atom prizes.
uncertainties: Hard to restrict credit to three people.
Relation to the 1997 and 2001 prizes on cooling and condensates.
